To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of in silico models for regulatory hazard assessment should be encouraged; (2) the current QSAR models for the REACH endpoints are not yet sufficiently reliable for the purpose of regulatory hazard assessment; (3) the use of QSAR models for regulatory hazard assessments should only be performed by experts with a thorough knowledge of both the science of QSAR modeling and the REACH legislation.
the application of QSAR models in REACH is a great opportunity for medicinal chemist, provided that the models are validated and the predictions are interpreted correctly.
• QSARs are a valuable tool for the prediction of toxicological properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
- The development of QSAR models to predict the toxicity of chemical compounds.
the application of QSAR models to predict the environmental toxicity of pharmaceuticals and other chemicals.
the application of in silico tools for the prediction of toxicity, and with the development of new tools to improve the prediction of toxicological endpoints.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
medicinal chemists are ideally positioned to contribute to a more sustainable chemical industry.
the application of in silico models in regulatory hazard assessment is a promising approach, provided that the models are properly validated and that their applicability domain is clearly defined.
the application of in silico approaches in medicinal chemistry is a reality and a necessity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of QSAR models in the regulatory context is still in its infancy, but the time is ripe for a breakthrough.
REACH and in silco methods are a very promising combination, which will provide new opportunities for the pharmaceutical industry.
the current state of predictive toxicology is such that it is already a valuable tool in the drug design process and will become more and more important in the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of in silico tools in the REACH process is a promising opportunity for medicinal chemist, but it is also a challenge that requires a multidisciplinary approach.
the use of QSAR models in REACH should be limited to endpoints that can be measured in vitro.
the use of in silico tools for the prediction of toxicological endpoints in REACH will be a challenging task.
